title: Bigger barns (Luke 12:13–21)
hook: a rich man plans his retirement and dies that night

segments.voice: Yesterday, a woman in the crowd blessed his mother, and he blessed everyone who keeps the word. Your line was hear and keep it. Which word did you keep? Day four hundred sixty-three, a new week.

It starts with a family fight. Someone in the crowd shouts at Jesus: Master, tell my brother to split the inheritance with me. Anyone who has watched siblings sit across a lawyer's table after a funeral knows the tone. Jesus refuses to be the judge. Who made me a divider over you? Then he turns to the crowd and says: beware of all covetousness, because a man's life does not consist in the abundance of things he possesses. And he tells them a story about a farmer whose year went very, very well. Today, the bigger barns.
screen: `TELL MY BROTHER TO SPLIT IT.` → `WHO MADE ME A DIVIDER?` → `A FARMER'S VERY GOOD YEAR.`

segments.voice: A rich man's land brings in a huge harvest. He has a problem most of us would like to have: nowhere to put it all. So he talks to himself, and Luke lets us listen. What shall I do? I know. I will pull down my barns and build greater, and store everything there. And I'll say to my soul: soul, you have plenty laid up for many years, take your rest, eat, drink, enjoy yourself. Notice who he's talking to. Only himself. My crops, my barns, my goods, my soul. Nobody else is in the room. Not his workers, not his neighbors, not the hungry, not God. Then God speaks into the room: "Thou fool, this night do they require thy soul of thee: and whose shall those things be which thou hast provided?" This night. Not in many years. Tonight. The man planned a retirement and didn't get an evening. And the question cuts back to the brothers fighting at the start: whose will it all be? Probably somebody's lawsuit. Jesus finishes: so is he that lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God. Notice he's not called a fool for having a good harvest or for planning ahead. Joseph stored grain in Egypt and saved lives. The man is a fool because the harvest only ever went into barns. Saint Basil the Great preached on this parable in the three hundreds, during a famine, and his point still lands: the extra bread you store belongs to the hungry, and the shoes rotting in your closet belong to someone barefoot. Catholics call this the universal destination of goods: what we own is meant, in the end, to serve everyone.
screen: `A HARVEST WITH NOWHERE TO GO.` · `MY CROPS, MY BARNS, MY SOUL.` · `RICH TOWARD GOD.` · `BASIL: THE EXTRA BREAD IS THEIRS.` · then, large: `THOU FOOL, THIS NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give away something stored up. Settle, and breathe. Picture your own barns: a closet, a garage, a drawer, a savings account, a pile of things you're keeping for someday. Walk through it in your mind slowly. Notice one thing that you aren't using and somebody else could. A coat, a set of tools, a book, an amount of money. Decide where it's going and when, today if you can. If you pray, ask to be rich toward God. The bell holds the time.
Bigger barns. The rich farmer's plan to store everything for himself, and God's answer: this night your soul is required of you. Today's word.
Your line: this night. Today, get one stored-up thing out of your barn and into someone's hands before you go to sleep. Day four hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the parable of the rich fool at Sunday Mass in the year of Luke's Gospel, and Catholic social teaching speaks of the universal destination of goods: private property is real, but its use is meant to serve the common good.

fork.setup: you're the farmer. your harvest is too big for your barns. what do you do?
options: tear them down and build bigger ones for yourself.
share the surplus with the village.
sell it all and buy more land.
fork.reveal: he builds bigger barns and plans years of ease. God says: this night your soul is required of thee.

original.note: Greek: fool, literally without understanding, one who doesn't think clearly about what matters.

trapdoor: what you thought: the parable says saving money is wrong.
what it means: the man's sin is that everything goes into his own barns and none of it toward God or neighbor.
what a scholar hears: aphron is the fool of Psalms and Proverbs, who acts as if God doesn't figure in his plans.
